name: Executive order of January 20, 1857 enlarging and moving the Nisqually Reservation under Article 6 of the Treaty of Medicine Creek
aka: Nisqually, Puyallup and Muckleshoot reservation order of 1857
citation: Executive order approved by the President January 20, 1857, under Article 6 of the Treaty of Medicine Creek of December 26, 1854
promises: Royce records that the President, as Article 6 of the Treaty of Medicine Creek allowed, changed the size and location of the reserves: the Nisqually reserve was enlarged and moved, the Puyallup reserve enlarged, and a new reserve established at Muckleshoot prairie.
Royce records that the Nisqually reserve as enlarged and moved by this order is the present Nisqually reserve.
The Nisqually Indian Tribe states that the enlargement gave a reservation of 4,717 acres on both sides of the river, in place of the 1,280 acres first set apart.

breaches.what: Congress authorized $85,000 in full settlement of the claims of twenty-five heads of families of the Nisqually Reservation, as compensation for the difference between the appraised value and the compromise price paid for about 3,300 acres of allotted land taken for military purposes, and for surrender of treaty rights and removal expenses.

source.title: Act of April 28, 1924, ch. 134, 43 Stat. 111 (relief of dispossessed allotted Indians of the Nisqually Reservation)

breaches.quote: approximately three thousand three hundred acres of allotted Indian land taken for military purposes, and for surrender of treaty rights and removal expenses

breaches.what: The Nisqually Indian Tribe states that in the winter of 1917 the U.S. Army moved onto Nisqually lands and ordered the people from their homes without warning, and that Pierce County condemned 3,353 acres of Nisqually land and transferred it to the Army to expand the Fort Lewis base.

landTaken: The Nisqually Indian Tribe states that Pierce County condemned 3,353 acres of Nisqually land for Fort Lewis; the 1924 Act describes approximately 3,300 acres of allotted land taken for military purposes.
compensation: HistoryLink (Paula Becker, essay 8005) states the Nisqually landholders were paid a small portion of their lands' value in April 1918 and that Congress provided some additional compensation in 1921. The Act of April 28, 1924 authorized $85,000 to be spent for the dispossessed families; whether and when it was appropriated and paid was not checked.
today: The Nisqually Indian Tribe states that the area north and east of the river is under the control of the Fort Lewis military base and serves as an impact area.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says its reservation was enlarged by executive order to 4,717 acres on both sides of the river, divided into 30 family allotments in 1884, and that in 1917 the Army ordered families from their homes and Pierce County condemned 3,353 acres for Fort Lewis.

sources.title: Charles C. Royce, Indian Land Cessions in the United States (18th Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 1899), schedule p. 818
Pierce County residents vote to purchase 70,000 acres, which will become Camp Lewis, on January 6, 1917 (Paula Becker, HistoryLink essay 8005)

openQuestions: This Royce record is an executive order that changed reserves under the 1854 Treaty of Medicine Creek, not a cession. Royce areas 405 and 406 appear to be the Puyallup enlargement and the moved Nisqually reserve; which number is which was not settled from the scanned schedule.
The same order also set up the Puyallup enlargement and the Muckleshoot reserve; those are not researched here.

The Nisqually Tribe dates the enlargement to an 1856 executive order; Royce and the Indian Claims Commission (Docket 197, 1973, quoting 1 Kappler 918-19) date the President's approval to January 20, 1857.

HistoryLink and Wikipedia report $65,000 appropriated in 1921; the Act found and opened is the Act of April 28, 1924 authorizing $85,000. Senate Document 243, 66th Congress, 2nd session (the Acting Secretary of the Interior's report of February 28, 1920) was not opened.
Indian Claims Commission Docket 197 (Nisqually) concerns the 1854 Medicine Creek cession and belongs with that treaty's record.

plain.promised: In 1857 the President enlarged and moved the Nisqually Reservation, as the Medicine Creek treaty allowed. The Tribe says it then held 4,717 acres on both sides of the river.
plain.happened: In 1917 the Army ordered Nisqually families from their homes, and Pierce County condemned 3,353 acres for Fort Lewis, the Tribe says. In 1924 Congress paid toward the land taken for military purposes and the surrender of treaty rights.
plain.today: Congress authorized $85,000 for the dispossessed families in 1924. The Tribe says the land north and east of the river is still part of the base.
